summary: You produced a working brute-force solution that passes most tests, and you correctly avoided using the same element twice by starting the inner loop at i+1. However, you missed an explicit edge-case requirement in the test suite (empty input/no-solution behavior), and you didn’t move to the expected O(n) hash-map solution for the given constraints (n up to 1e5).

primary_focus: Implement the canonical single-pass hash-map Two Sum pattern (and keep a simple return-[] fallback) so your solution is both scalable and aligned with typical test harness contracts.
thinking_and_logic: You chose the brute-force nested-loop approach and were careful about distinct indices by starting the inner loop at i+1, which addresses the common pitfall of using the same element twice. You noted the existence of an O(n) hash map approach but didn’t transition to it, which matters given the large n constraint. The edge-case miss came from relying on the “exactly one valid answer exists” constraint while the tests still included an empty-input expectation, so the function’s contract didn’t match the harness.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the ANSWER KEY brute_force approach (O(n^2) time, O(1) space) and therefore does not meet the expected scalability for n up to 1e5 where the ANSWER KEY optimal approach is a single pass with a hash map (seen value -> index) for O(n) time. Functionally, the only observed failing behavior is the decision to raise ValueError on empty/no-solution input, while the tests expect an empty list; adding a guard and returning [] would address the failing edge test. Moving to the hash-map pattern would also align with typical interview expectations and avoid timeouts in larger hidden cases even if they didn’t appear here.

next_steps.action: Rewrite Two Sum using the single-pass hash map (seen values -> index; check complement before insert).
next_steps.why: This is the canonical optimal solution: O(n) time instead of O(n^2), which is necessary for arrays up to 1e5.
next_steps.how: Iterate i, x in enumerate(nums): let c = target - x; if c in seen return [seen[c], i]; else seen[x] = i.

Writing the nested loops now. Outer loop i, inner loop from i plus one so I don't reuse the same element.
Okay, it works on the example. Running the visible tests.
Before you finish — consider whether there are any unusual inputs worth checking.
Unusual inputs... duplicates should be fine since I use indices. I think I'm good, submitting.
